doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Live electronics and PASS studio
summary: Her interest in electronics, learning at the Public Access Synthesizer Studio, and studio setup time.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Are you a fan of technology?

Yeah. Live electronics are an important part of my music, and something I’ve always been interested in, something I’ve never been afraid of or ever thought that it was any kind of contradiction to the life and thought of a jazz musician. It’s just interesting to me.
Yeah. How did that first happen? To say hey, this is cool stuff here.

I think I was just always interested in electronic music, got exposed to it in college, met musicians in New York who were a little more technically minded than I was, taught me about how to use effects processing. There was an electronics music studio in New York that was set up to help musicians get access to new equipment called PASS, Public Access Synthesizer Studio, which now has turned into Harvest Works.

At the time, we’re talking 15 years ago, a very interesting place because that’s a place where I learned, I got a chance to learn about how to handle and work around with electronics and get a feel for it. And now, well the whole world of computers and electronics has changed drastically since then, but it was my introduction.
Does it add to the time you need in the studio to take advantage of the electronics that you want to?

Well if I bring my own live electronics set-up, you have to spend a lot more time setting it up, making sure that all the lines are clear and all the things that can go wrong won’t go wrong. So it gets a little more — it’s not that bad, but just a few more input lines. You have to sort of make sure everything is A-okay.
